clue.text: Everyone inhabiting trees is getting there first

indicators.note: whatever inhabits a place lives inside it, so one word sits within the other

blocks.note: a mass of trees makes forests
everyone is all

explanation.surface: Some creature living among the trees manages to arrive ahead of everyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive-looking final S of the trees word lets the other piece slip in just before it.
explanation.definitionFit: To forestall is to act in advance and so prevent a rival, which is beating them to the spot.

clue.text: State musicians stay up for European

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading the letters from bottom to top

blocks.note: VA is the postal abbreviation for Virginia, a US state
the London Symphony Orchestra
a guy is a rope that stays a tent or mast

explanation.surface: Players from some state are asked to stay on for a European tour.
explanation.walkthrough: VA, LSO and GUY run together as VALSOGUY, and the whole string is turned upward to read YUGOSLAV.
explanation.definitionFit: A Yugoslav was a native of the former Balkan federation, so the word names a kind of European person.

blocks.note: in cricket the on side is also called the leg side
an ion is an atom carrying an electric charge

explanation.walkthrough: 'On charge' reads like a battery or an accused person; it is two separate pieces. The leg side is the half of a cricket field behind the batter's legs.
explanation.definitionFit: Legion as an adjective means very numerous, as in the phrase 'their name is legion'.

indicators.note: something rising in a down entry is read from the bottom up

blocks.note: the Met is London's Metropolitan Police; the possessive adds the S

explanation.surface: A call to halt an increase in the strength of the police.
explanation.walkthrough: The Met is the everyday name for London's Metropolitan Police.
explanation.definitionFit: To stem a flow is to check or halt it, as when a bandage stems bleeding.

clue.text: How the Tour de France comes round?

definitions.text: How the Tour de France comes round?

blocks.clueFragment: How the Tour de France comes round?
blocks.note: surface reading: the bike race returns once a year, in a regular rhythm
setter's reading: the race is ridden on bicycles, so it travels by cycle

explanation.surface: Musing on the famous bike race recurring each summer.
explanation.walkthrough: The adverb describes both an annual recurrence and a journey made on cycles, which the riders literally use.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that happens in cycles returns at regular intervals, as the yearly race does, and bicycles are cycles.

indicators.note: something strange is out of its usual order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: rearranged
to set is to put down

explanation.surface: A shire is placed beneath some peculiar local customs.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'under' places SET below the rearranged letters. Somerset is a county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Somerset is one of the administrative shires of England, lying south of Bristol.

blocks.note: first meaning: a nation, the second largest in the world by area
second meaning: Lake Superior lies along this nation's frontier with the USA

explanation.surface: A boast that one nation's frontier beats everyone else's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Superior' looks like a boast; it is Lake Superior, the largest of the Great Lakes, which straddles the frontier.
explanation.definitionFit: The nation north of the United States shares the Great Lakes boundary, including Lake Superior, with it.

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the letters are read from bottom to top

blocks.note: N is the chemical symbol for nitrogen
the Dee is a river in Wales and England, and another in Scotland

explanation.surface: A lack of nitrogen in the water further upstream.
explanation.definitionFit: Need as a noun means a lack or want of something, a deficiency.

indicators.note: a tune that is played is performed with its notes worked over, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: Polly performs a melody while living the high life.
explanation.definitionFit: Opulently means richly and lavishly, with the abundance that luxury implies.

clue.text: In search for a teapot spout

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the following words, spanning their letters

blocks.note: surface padding, giving no letters
running across the gaps between words

explanation.surface: Hunting around for the pouring nozzle of a teapot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spout' looks like part of the teapot; it is the verb meaning to speechify.
explanation.definitionFit: To spout is to hold forth at length, and to orate is to make a pompous speech.

clue.text: Self-centredness: somehow it goes to my head

indicators.note: somehow says the letters arrive in some unspecified order, so they are rearranged
the head of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: rearranged
the opening letter

explanation.surface: Vanity described as something that goes to one's head.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is 'it goes'; 'to' joins it to the M taken from 'my'.
explanation.definitionFit: Egotism is excessive preoccupation with oneself, which is what being self-centred means.

clue.text: Pull fish back to where the wind blows

indicators.note: going back means the letters are read from right to left

blocks.note: to draw is to pull
an eel is a fish

explanation.surface: Hauling in a catch and heading off downwind.
explanation.definitionFit: Leeward is the sailing term for the side or direction away from the wind, towards which it blows.

clue.text: Vicious hooker, member of the Eagles

blocks.note: first meaning: a sharp curved claw that hooks prey
second meaning: a limb part belonging to a bird of prey

explanation.surface: A violent rugby forward who plays for a team called the Eagles.
explanation.walkthrough: A hooker is a rugby position, and the Eagles sounds like a sports team or a band; both are misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: A talon is the hooked claw of a raptor, a cruel gripping weapon on each foot of the bird.

blocks.note: to second a motion is to back it
a stage is a floor or level of a building

explanation.surface: Directions to the second storey, out of public view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second floor' reads as one storey of a building; it is two words, a verb and a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Backstage means in the area behind a theatre's set, out of the audience's sight, so figuratively in private.

clue.text: One whose life is in books

definitions.text: One whose life is in books

blocks.clueFragment: One whose life is in books
blocks.note: surface reading: a bookworm who lives for reading
setter's reading: the life is someone else's, which this writer sets down in print

explanation.surface: A devoted reader who seems to live inside books.
explanation.walkthrough: The life in the books is not the writer's own but that of the person written about.
explanation.definitionFit: This author writes accounts of other people's lives, so a subject's life ends up in the author's volumes.

clue.text: Daring printers experimenting with two Es

indicators.note: experimenting means trying things in new arrangements, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written
two copies of the letter E

explanation.surface: Bold typesetters try out a pair of extra vowels.
explanation.definitionFit: Enterprise as a noun means boldness and initiative, the quality of being daring in business or action.

blocks.note: first meaning: a major railway terminus in the City of London
second meaning, by example: a road on Merseyside made famous by the Beatles

explanation.surface: Asking which railway stop serves the road made famous by the Beatles.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second meaning as an example: Penny Lane is one road in the Beatles' home city. The station is in London, nowhere near it.
explanation.definitionFit: The London terminus is named this, and Penny Lane is literally one thoroughfare in the Beatles' home city on Merseyside.

clue.text: Daughter, perhaps, at the end of her Ecstasy

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

blocks.note: the final letter
ecstasy is great joy, elation

explanation.surface: A girl finally overcome with joy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ecstasy' suggests the drug, often abbreviated E; here it is the full word for rapture.
explanation.definitionFit: A daughter is one example of a family member, a relative or relation; 'perhaps' flags the example.

indicators.note: a broken thing is in pieces that can be put back in a different order

blocks.note: rearranged
a fellow is a man

explanation.surface: A lovelorn chap is called on by the film alien.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue describes the kind of person an alien would come calling on. ET is the alien in Spielberg's film, who visits our planet.
explanation.definitionFit: An earthman is an inhabitant of our planet as seen from space, the kind of person an alien visitor meets.

indicators.note: emptying a word removes its contents, leaving only the outside letters

blocks.note: a scholar is a student
the first and last letters

explanation.surface: A clever pupil has cleared out the library.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Learned' is the two-syllable adjective, not the past tense of learn.
explanation.definitionFit: Scholarly describes someone with deep academic knowledge, which is what a learned person has.

indicators.note: only some of the following letters are used, a run inside them

blocks.note: running across the gap between the words

explanation.surface: A remark that certain phones send signals straight through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Direct' looks like a verb or a description of transmission; it is the adjective meaning frank.
explanation.definitionFit: Being direct means speaking plainly and frankly, without deceit, which is being truthful.

clue.text: A successful doctor is also a smoker

blocks.note: first meaning: one who restores patients to health
second meaning: one who preserves fish or meat by smoking it

explanation.surface: A thriving medic who happens to light up cigarettes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smoker' suggests a tobacco user; here it is someone who preserves food over smoke.
explanation.definitionFit: A healer brings about recovery, and a food processor preserves bacon or kippers by salting and smoking them.

clue.text: Where the projectionist came in reeling?

definitions.text: Where the projectionist came in reeling?

indicators.note: reeling means staggering about, so the letters lurch into a new order

blocks.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: The film operator staggered into work, perhaps drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue describes the place a projectionist arrives at to spin reels of film.
explanation.definitionFit: A projectionist works in a picture house, entering it to run reels of film for the audience.

blocks.note: first meaning: an express train that makes no halts
second meaning: a sentence lacking any full stop

explanation.surface: A command to state something without commas or full stops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Express' looks like a verb meaning to put into words; it is the fast train.
explanation.definitionFit: An express service runs through without halting, and text lacking any full stop literally has no stop.

indicators.note: awa is Scots for away, so the letters are sent off out of their places

blocks.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: A Scots order to see off some troublemakers.
explanation.walkthrough: Ned is Scottish slang for a young thug, matching the Scots word awa.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scottish slang a ned is a young lout or petty delinquent, so the plural means troublemakers.

blocks.note: Peter Pan, the boy who never grew up
taken as written
R stands for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: Hailing someone called Peter as monarch of the felines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peter, the King' reads like a royal title; Peter clues his famous surname.
explanation.definitionFit: A panther is a big wild feline, usually a black leopard or a puma.

blocks.note: first meaning: to cram or squeeze tightly
second meaning: the forwards of a rugby team, who bind in the scrum

explanation.walkthrough: 'Press forwards' sounds like an order to advance; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: To pack is to compress or cram, and in rugby the eight scrummaging players are collectively called the pack.

clue.text: A dance very lacking in invention

indicators.note: lacking means going without, so those letters are taken away

blocks.note: taken as written, to be removed
a discovery is a find or invention

explanation.surface: A dance routine with hardly any originality.
explanation.walkthrough: Take VERY off the end of DISCOVERY to leave DISCO.
explanation.definitionFit: A disco is a party or event with dancing to recorded pop music, so it stands for a dance.

indicators.note: something tormented is twisted about, so the letters are wrenched into a new order

blocks.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: Causing a seizure in someone already in agony.
explanation.definitionFit: To encompass a result is an old sense meaning to contrive or achieve it, so it means cause to happen.
